identification.title: You Are My Hiding Place
identification.notes: Written by Michael Ledner in 1981, published by Maranatha! Music. A short Scripture chorus built on Psalm 32:7, from the era when much congregational song was set directly from the text.

claims.structuralNotes: A single short chorus, sung through repeatedly, with no verses. Its lines follow Psalm 32:7 closely and then add a resolution to trust.

claims.claim: God is the singer's hiding place.
claims.subject: God as refuge

claims.claim: God surrounds the singer with songs of deliverance.
claims.subject: Deliverance

claims.claim: When afraid, the singer will trust God.
claims.subject: Faith in fear

claims.claim: The weak may call themselves strong in the Lord's strength.
claims.subject: Strength in weakness

strengths.title: A psalm set almost unaltered
strengths.explanation: The chorus follows Psalm 32:7 closely enough that a congregation singing it has the verse in their mouths. The song's best material is not the songwriter's, which is the right kind of borrowing.
strengths.scriptureRationale: You are a hiding place for me; you surround me with shouts of deliverance.

strengths.title: Trust stated as a decision, not a feeling
strengths.explanation: The line about fear resolves into a choice rather than a mood. It gives a frightened singer something to do rather than something to feel, which is what the psalms model.
strengths.scriptureRationale: When I am afraid, I put my trust in you — the same decision under the same condition.

strengths.title: Strength located in God rather than found within
strengths.explanation: The weak are not told they are secretly strong; they are told to say so on the strength of someone else's. The distinction is small in words and large in meaning.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Let the weak say, I am strong — the line the song borrows, and it is a claim about God's strength.

doctrinesAffirmed: Trust as a decision under fear
theological.assessment: A short psalm-chorus that does exactly what it sets out to do. Its material is Scripture's own, it turns fear into a decision rather than a feeling, and it locates strength outside the singer. There is nothing here to correct. What limits it is scope rather than accuracy: four lines about refuge, with nothing about who God is beyond that or what he has done to become one.

strengths.title: Learned in a single pass
strengths.explanation: Four lines, a narrow melody and no arrangement to depend on. It works unaccompanied and in a small room, which is where songs like this earn their keep.

strengths.title: Fits someone who is frightened
strengths.explanation: The song asks nothing of the singer's composure and names fear directly. For a congregation in a hard week it gives them a short true thing to hold.

concerns.title: Sung in the singular
concerns.explanation: The psalm behind it is a personal confession and the song keeps that. A congregation sings alongside one another rather than as one voice, which suits the text but limits it corporately.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in D and E. A narrow melody with short phrases; among the easiest songs in use for a mixed room.

range.key: Commonly published in D and E
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: One chorus repeated — the form of a Scripture chorus rather than a fault. What repeats is a psalm verse, so it puts Scripture in the mouth rather than filling time.
communal.assessment: About as easy as congregational singing gets, and built to be repeated. It carries unaccompanied, names fear honestly and gives a frightened room four true lines. Its only communal limitation is the singular voice it inherits from the psalm.

strengths.title: Four plain lines, nothing to interpret
strengths.explanation: The images are concrete and biblical, and every phrase lands complete on the first hearing. A child follows it.

concerns.title: The one addressed is never named
concerns.explanation: The song runs entirely on 'You'. The refuge imagery is biblical enough to make the intent plain inside a church, but nothing in the words names God, so the identification is supplied by the setting rather than the text.

clarity.assessment: Plain throughout, and its imagery is specific enough to be recognisably biblical. The one gap is that God is never named — carried here by the psalm's language rather than left wholly open, but carried nonetheless.

synthesis.summary: A four-line psalm-chorus that does exactly what it sets out to do: Scripture's own words, fear turned into a decision rather than a feeling, and strength located outside the singer. Nothing here to correct. What limits it is scope — four lines about refuge, with nothing about what God has done to become one.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The verse the chorus sets almost unaltered.
Trust as the decision made under fear, which the song repeats.
Let the weak say I am strong — borrowed, and about God's strength rather than the singer's.
